Larcenous means of, relating to, characterized by, or involving theft. It is the adjective form of the noun larceny, which is the legal term for the deliberate, wrongful taking of someone else's property with the intention of keeping it permanently. So when you attach the word "larcenous" to something, you are saying it has the quality, nature, or character of theft.

Think of it this way: larceny is the crime, and larcenous is the word that says something belongs to or smells like that crime.
What Can Be Described as Larcenous?

The word is flexible — it can describe a person, an action, an intention, or a scheme.

A person. Calling someone larcenous means they are thieving by nature, habit, or tendency. It paints them as someone whose character is that of a thief — someone with a constant impulse or history of stealing.

"The larcenous pickpocket worked his way through the crowded marketplace."

An act or behavior. An action is larcenous if it constitutes theft or is built around stealing.

"The employee's larcenous behavior — pocketing cash from the register — went unnoticed for months."

An intention or motive. In legal language especially, the phrase larcenous intent is very important. It refers to the deliberate, conscious purpose of stealing — meaning the person knew the property wasn't theirs and meant to permanently take it anyway. Without this intent, the act may not legally qualify as larceny at all.

"The defense argued that there was no larcenous intent — the defendant genuinely believed the bicycle was abandoned."

A plan or scheme. Any plot or strategy designed around stealing can be called larcenous.

"They devised a larcenous scheme to siphon funds from the company over several years."
The Figurative Use — When Nothing Is Actually Stolen

Beyond its strict, legal meaning, larcenous is also used figuratively in everyday language to describe something that feels like robbery — usually because of extreme unfairness, exploitation, or outrageous pricing. In this use, no actual crime is taking place, but the speaker is dramatizing how unjust or excessive something is.

"Those ticket service fees are absolutely larcenous!"
"The hotel charged a larcenous amount for a tiny bottle of water."

This figurative use is common and completely acceptable. It adds sharpness and color to language. When someone calls a price "larcenous," they mean it's so unreasonably high that it might as well be theft.
An Important Distinction — What Larcenous Does NOT Imply

This is where the razor-sharp accuracy matters.

Larcenous does not mean violent. Larceny is specifically a non-violent crime. The moment theft involves physical force, threats, or intimidation against a person, it becomes robbery — a different and more serious crime. Larcenous, therefore, carries no implication of violence or physical confrontation. It is purely about taking what isn't yours.

Larcenous does not mean accidental. The idea of intention is built into the word. If someone genuinely mistakes another person's umbrella for their own and walks off with it, that is not larcenous — there was no intent to steal. Larcenous always implies a knowing, deliberate act of taking.
The Scale of the Theft Doesn't Change the Word

Larceny legally comes in two broad degrees — petty larceny (small-scale theft, like stealing a phone) and grand larceny (large-scale theft, like stealing a car or a large sum of money). The adjective larcenous applies equally to both ends of the scale. Whether the theft is trivial or enormous, the word larcenous can describe it without any change in meaning.

• Larceny (noun) — the act of theft itself: "He was charged with grand larceny."
  • Larcenously (adverb) — in a thieving manner: "She larcenously helped herself to her colleague's credit card details."
The Complete Picture in One Sentence

Larcenous describes anything — a person, an action, a plan, or a motive — that is characterized by deliberate, non-violent theft, or that resembles theft in its unfairness; and figuratively, it describes anything so outrageously excessive that it feels like stealing.
